content: It encourages a culture where every employee feels empowered and responsible for safety, effectively merging the requirements of regulatory compliance with the ethos of a genuine safety culture. The regulations, in this view, provide the minimum baseline, while the management system provides the framework for striving towards "Goal Zero" or zero harm. Central to the success of any safety system, and a core tenet of the MHSA, is the principle of competence . The law requires that any person performing a task that could affect health and safety must be properly trained and declared competent to do so. For drill-and-blast operations, this is of paramount importance. The blaster-in-charge must hold a valid Blasting Ticket , a certification issued by the DMRE after a rigorous process of theoretical training, practical experience under supervision, and examination. This is the ultimate license for an individual to handle and use explosives. Ongoing, documented refresher training is also critical to maintain competence and ensure that the workforce is up-to-date with new technologies, procedures, and regulatory changes. In synthesis, the regulatory and safety environment in South Africa is a defining feature of the drill-and-blast market. It is a complex, multi-layered system of legal obligations, stringent enforcement, and high expectations from clients and society. Navigating this landscape successfully requires more than just a passing familiarity with the law; it demands a dedicated, expert-led compliance function, a significant investment in safety systems and training, and an unwavering organizational commitment to a culture of zero harm. The high barriers to entry created by this regulatory framework serve to filter out unprepared or unscrupulous operators, but for a company like Veralogix that is prepared to meet and exceed these standards, a strong safety record and a sophisticated compliance system can become a powerful competitive advantage. Mining companies are under intense scrutiny from investors, regulators, and communities to improve their environmental performance and demonstrate their social license to operate. This pressure flows directly down to their contractors. In the drill-and-blast sector, this translates into a demand for "greener" blasting practices.
